entries.clue: Admirable warhorse, pity it's injured (12)

indicatorNotes.injured: an injured thing is knocked out of shape, so the letters are too

annotation.surface: A brave old warhorse has been hurt, and the onlooker feels sorry for it.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma splits the surface into two statements, but 'warhorse, pity' is one run of letters to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: Something praiseworthy deserves admiration, so it is admirable.

entries.clue: Dispense liquid from the pump ourselves (4)

indicatorNotes.from: the answer is taken out of the words that follow

annotation.surface: Filling up at the pump without an attendant: we serve ourselves.
annotation.walkthrough: The pump makes 'Dispense liquid' look like part of a petrol-station scene, while the answer sits across the gap between two words.
annotation.definitionFit: To pour is to let liquid flow out of a container.

entries.clue: Nearly everyone has trees and plants up high (7)

indicatorNotes.Nearly: nearly all of a word: drop its last letter

annotation.surface: Almost everybody keeps trees and plants somewhere elevated.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Up high' seems to describe where the plants are kept, but it is part of the definition: these are mountain plants.
annotation.definitionFit: A gardener's term: alpines are plants native to mountain slopes above the tree line, grown in rock gardens.

entries.clue: Loose rocks almost put on television (5)

indicatorNotes.almost: almost the whole word: its last letter goes

blocks.note: 'put on television' is to broadcast, a six-letter verb, cut short by one letter

annotation.surface: Some loose rocks nearly got broadcast on TV.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Put on television' is a verb here: to SCREEN a programme is to broadcast it, and dropping the N leaves the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Scree is the mass of loose stones on a mountain slope.

entries.clue: Metal ring to get cleaner (6)

blocks.note: a flat ring fitted under a nut or bolt head
a noun here: one who cleans with water

annotation.surface: A metal ring needs a scrub to come out cleaner.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cleaner' reads as a comparative adjective, but it is a noun: a person or machine that cleans.
annotation.definitionFit: A washer is both a ring spacing a bolt and something that washes.

entries.clue: Right to pass by recurrence of illness (7)

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right

annotation.surface: A right of way lets you pass, though here it comes with a returning sickness.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pass by' looks like one phrasal verb, but only 'to pass' is the wordplay; 'by' just links it to the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A relapse is falling ill again after seeming to recover.

entries.clue: Skeins of yarn for Tom? (5)

blocks.note: a famous Hollywood actor's first name

annotation.surface: Wool bought as a present for someone called Tom.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that Tom is a particular Tom, the film actor, and HANKS is his surname.
annotation.definitionFit: Hanks are loose coils of yarn, and Hanks is Tom's surname.

entries.clue: Decoration had shortly, we hear, been interfered with (7)

annotation.definitionNote: MEDDLED is active (had meddled with); the clue's passive phrasing fits only loosely

indicatorNotes.we hear: the result is what we hear, not what is written

blocks.note: MEDAL, a decoration, plus 'D, a short 'had'

annotation.surface: A medal someone had turns out, by rumour, to have been tampered with.
annotation.walkthrough: MEDAL'D and MEDDLED are pronounced alike, so the soundalike carries the whole answer.
annotation.definitionFit: To meddle is to interfere in something that is not your concern.

entries.clue: Some suppers contain stimulant (5)

indicatorNotes.Some: only some of the letters are used
indicatorNotes.contain: the answer is held inside the word

annotation.surface: Certain evening meals have a pick-me-up in them.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests caffeine in the food; the stimulant is literally inside the word 'suppers'.
annotation.definitionFit: Slang: a drug that lifts your mood and energy is called an upper, the opposite of a downer.

entries.clue: Gag because the Parisian is inside (7)

indicatorNotes.is inside: one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: French for 'the'; it goes inside the other piece

annotation.surface: A joke works because a man from Paris is in on it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gag' looks like a joke, but it is the verb: to gag someone is to silence them.
annotation.definitionFit: To gag someone is to stop them speaking, to silence them.

entries.clue: Deprived of light, person exuded instability (12)

indicatorNotes.instability: unstable letters shift out of order

annotation.surface: Someone kept in the dark gives off an air of being unbalanced.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a person's mental state; 'Deprived of light' is the photographer's sense instead.
annotation.definitionFit: An underexposed photograph received too little light.

entries.clue: Picture a Lennon song (7)

blocks.note: a verb here: to see in the mind's eye

annotation.surface: An invitation to picture one of John Lennon's songs.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Picture' reads as a noun, a painting or photo, but it is the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: To picture is to imagine, and Imagine is Lennon's best-known solo song.

entries.clue: Religious book from girl, a novice (6)

blocks.note: L for learner, as on a learner driver's L-plate

annotation.surface: A girl new to the faith is given a book of prayers.
annotation.walkthrough: L stands for learner because British learner drivers must display an L-plate.
annotation.definitionFit: A missal is the book containing the prayers of the Catholic Mass.

entries.clue: Al leaves Down Under for another country (7)

indicatorNotes.leaves: AL departs from the word, taking its letters with it

blocks.note: 'Down Under' is Australia; the letters A and L come out of it

annotation.surface: A man named Al emigrates from Australia to a new country.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' pretends Al is travelling; really AL drops out of AUSTRALIA, which is why the answer is 'another' country.
annotation.definitionFit: Defined by example: Austria is one country, and 'another' nods to the Australia it was carved from.

entries.clue: Save tree centre with broken cues (6)

indicatorNotes.centre: take the middle of the word
indicatorNotes.broken: broken into bits, the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the middle two letters of tREe

annotation.surface: A snooker player saves the centre of a tree with some broken cues.
annotation.walkthrough: The centre of a four-letter word is its middle two letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to save someone from danger is to rescue them.

entries.clue: Use clinker to twist into folds (7)

indicatorNotes.Use: the letters of CLINKER are put to work, reshaped into a new word

annotation.surface: Instructions for bending a lump of furnace clinker into ridges.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Twist' is the obvious anagram signal, but it belongs to the definition; the rearranging is done by 'Use'. Clinker is the stony residue left in a furnace.
annotation.definitionFit: To crinkle something is to crease it into small folds and wrinkles.

entries.clue: He'd captured member and caused injury (6)

annotation.definitionNote: HARMED normally takes an object; 'caused injury' is the intransitive version

indicatorNotes.captured: one piece holds the other captive inside it

blocks.note: a limb, a member of the body; it goes inside the other piece

annotation.surface: A man grabbed someone's arm and hurt them.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Member' reads as someone in a club, but it is the old sense of a limb.
annotation.definitionFit: To harm someone is to injure them.

entries.clue: Cunning practice smashing me and pa to pieces (12)

indicatorNotes.to pieces: smashed to pieces, the letters are scattered and rebuilt

blocks.note: anagram fodder: SMASHING, ME and PA, 12 letters

annotation.surface: A sly trick that beats both me and my dad hollow.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Smashing' looks like the anagram indicator, but it is fodder; 'to pieces' does the rearranging.
annotation.definitionFit: Gamesmanship is winning by artful tricks that stop just short of cheating.

entries.clue: Mother with boy, stoneworker (5)

annotation.surface: A mother and her son run the family stonemasonry.
annotation.walkthrough: Family words are crossword staples: mother is MA or MUM, boy is SON or LAD, and here they simply sit side by side.
annotation.definitionFit: A mason cuts and builds with stone.

entries.clue: Dine on ship's chairs (5)

indicatorNotes.on: on board: the first piece goes aboard the ship

blocks.note: to dine; it goes aboard, between the two letters of the ship

annotation.surface: Having dinner on board, in the ship's chairs.
annotation.walkthrough: SS, for steamship, is the standard prefix of a ship's name.
annotation.definitionFit: Chairs are one kind of seat, a definition by example.

entries.clue: Change text in published itinerary (4)

indicatorNotes.in: the answer lies in the words that follow

annotation.surface: Correcting the wording of a travel schedule that has already gone to print.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer spans the join between the two words, which is easy to miss when reading them as a phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an editor's job is revising and correcting written copy.

entries.clue: Dodgy remedy for guitar ban? (7)

blocks.note: strumming is how a guitar is played

annotation.surface: A quack cure offered to anyone who wants guitar playing stopped.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the stretch: a guitar ban would read as 'no strum'.
annotation.definitionFit: A nostrum is a quack medicine of doubtful worth.

entries.clue: Enquired about a desk (5)

annotation.surface: Someone made enquiries about buying a desk.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Enquired about' reads as one phrase, but 'about' belongs to the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to enquire is the more formal word for putting a question.

entries.clue: Livid about Peruvian heritage (12)

blocks.note: the Inca empire was centred on Peru

annotation.surface: Someone is furious about their Peruvian ancestry.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Livid about' reads as one phrase, but 'about' is only the join. The Inca were the empire of the Andes, centred on Peru.
annotation.definitionFit: Incandescent with rage means livid, burning with anger.
